findings.heading: Descriptive analysis
findings.proposition: The recommended summary statistic for households per cluster and individuals per household is the MEDIAN with its range; the Portuguese states it is the MEAN ('Numero medio') with an interval.
findings.reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader reports the mean number of households per cluster instead of the median, which is the statistic the handbook recommends for these skewed cluster-survey counts, so the reported summary is inflated by large households and is not comparable with reports following the English guidance.

findings.heading: Demographic pyramids
findings.proposition: The English tells the reader to consult the help page `?plot_age_pyramid` for details of the `stack_by` argument; the Portuguese tells the reader to consult `?age_pyramid`.
findings.reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader opens a different help page from the one the English chapter points to, so the two language versions document the `stack_by` argument from different packages (sitrep vs apyramid) and a reader following one cannot reproduce the other's reference.

findings.heading: Weighted proportions > Survey package
findings.proposition: `svymean()` is used to extract an appropriate DESIGN EFFECT; the Portuguese says it extracts an appropriate DESIGN ('Um delineamento apropriado pode ser extraido utilizando o `svymean()`').
findings.reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader is told that svymean() produces a survey design, which it does not. The reader loses the reason to call svymean() with deff = TRUE and may not realise the design effect is the quantity being obtained.

findings.heading: Weighted proportions
findings.proposition: The tables carry confidence intervals and the DESIGN EFFECT; the Portuguese lists only 'intervalos de confianca associados e delineamento' (design), omitting 'effect'.
findings.reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader does not learn that the tables in this section report a design effect, so does not look for or interpret that column, even though the code beside it computes deff.

findings.heading: Weighted proportions
findings.proposition: **srvyr** fits most nicely within TIDYVERSE work-flows; the Portuguese says only that srvyr 'cabera melhor dentro do fluxos de trabalho' (fits better within work-flows), dropping tidyverse.
findings.reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader loses the criterion for choosing srvyr over survey, which is that srvyr suits tidyverse pipelines, and reads it as a vague claim that srvyr fits workflows better in general.

findings.heading: Survey design objects
findings.proposition: **srvyr** is a wrapper that makes TIDYVERSE-FRIENDLY objects and functions; the Portuguese says it 'torna os objetos e funcoes mais faceis de arrumar' (makes objects and functions easier to tidy up).
findings.reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader does not learn that srvyr exists to give tidyverse-compatible objects, so cannot connect this package choice to the dplyr piping used throughout the rest of the chapter.

findings.heading: Sampling bias
findings.proposition: It is INCREASING sample size that leads to differences that may be irrelevant after weighting; the Portuguese says only 'o tamanho da amostra levara' (the sample size will lead to).
findings.reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader misses the reason the binomial p-values are only indicative, which is that larger samples make trivial differences significant, and may therefore treat a significant p-value in a large survey as evidence of real sampling bias.
